prerequisites: It is highly recommended to have previously taken and passed the Machine Mechanics course from the 2nd year, 1st semester; it is also advisable to have passed Physics I and Mathematics from the first year.

learning_outcomes.text: Students must have the ability to gather and interpret relevant data (usually within their field of study) to make judgments that include a reflection on relevant social, scientific or ethical issues.
Students must have developed those learning skills necessary to undertake further studies with a high degree of autonomy.

Students must know how to apply their knowledge to their work or vocation in a professional manner and possess the competencies that are usually demonstrated through the elaboration and defense of arguments and the resolution of problems within their field of study.
Students must be able to transmit information, ideas, problems and solutions to both specialized and non-specialized audiences.
Applied knowledge of manufacturing systems and processes, metrology and quality control.
Knowledge and capacities for the calculation, design and testing of machines.
Knowledge and capacities to apply the fundamentals of elasticity and strength of materials to the behavior of real solids.
Knowledge and capacities for the calculation and design of industrial structures and constructions.
Knowledge and capacities for the design, analysis and calculation of mechanisms and mechanical systems.
Ability to transmit information orally and in writing adapted to the audience.
Ability to apply new technologies, including information and communication technologies.
Ability to manage information, handle and apply technical specifications and necessary legislation for engineering practice.

syllabus_topics: Topic 1: Introduction. Particle kinematics and relative motion.
Basic concepts: position, velocity and acceleration.
Determination of the motion of a particle.
Rectangular components of velocity and acceleration.
Motion relative to a translating reference frame.
Motion of a particle in space: cylindrical coordinates.
Topic 2: Rigid body kinematics and relative motion.
Introduction. Types of rigid body motion.
Motion relative to a rotating reference frame.
Topic 3: Fundamental concepts of machine and mechanism theory.
Determination of the degree of freedom.
Topic 4: Kinematic analysis of planar mechanisms.
Analytical solutions for velocity with vector loop.
Analytical solutions for acceleration with vector loop.
Dimensional synthesis of elementary planar mechanisms.
Topic 5: Particle kinetics I: Newton's Second Law.
Motion under a central force. Conservation of angular momentum.
Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation. Weight on Earth's surface.
Topic 6: Particle kinetics II: Energy and momentum methods.
Kinetic energy of a particle. Work and energy principle.
Topic 7: Kinetics of systems of particles.
Angular momentum of a system of particles with respect to its center of mass.
Kinetic energy and potential energy. Conservation of energy.
Topic 8: Rigid body kinetics I: Forces and accelerations.
Equations of motion of the rigid body.
Angular momentum of a rigid body.
Plane motion of the rigid body.
Topic 9: Rigid body kinetics II: Energy and momentum methods.
Work of forces and couples acting on a rigid body.
Kinetic energy of a rigid body. Work and energy principle.
Impulse and momentum principle for a rigid body.
Procedure for analysis of vibrating systems.
Complex number representation of harmonic motion.
Topic 11: Free vibrations of single degree of freedom systems.
Free vibration of an undamped system.
Topic 12: Forced vibrations of single degree of freedom systems.
Response of an undamped system subjected to a harmonic force.
Response of a damped system subjected to a harmonic force.
E: KINEMATICS OF CAMS AND GEARS:
Topic 13: Kinematic design of cams and gears.
Gear kinematics: Fundamental law of gearing.
Practice 1: Kinematic study of particles by numerical methods.
Practice 2: Numerical kinematic calculation of a mechanism.
Practice 3: Kinematic simulation of mechanisms with CAD software.
Practice 4: Resolution of non-linear kinetic problems.
Practice 5: Experimental analysis of 1 degree of freedom vibrations.
teaching_methods: Lectures: Exposition of theoretical knowledge, general problem-solving methods, and resolution of typical exercises.
Practice group classes: Application of new computational and experimental technologies for course content analysis through simulation activities and laboratory experiences.
Collective tutorials: Seminars or collective doubt-resolution sessions to address collateral aspects for the correct assimilation of course content.

assessment_methods.method: Attendance and/or participation in in-person and/or virtual activities
Written exam on theoretical-practical concepts of the subject
Completion of assignments, cases or exercises
Laboratory/field practices/use of ICT tools (attendance and submission of practice reports)

assessment_rules: The grading system will be governed by RD 1125/2003. Evaluation is primarily through a written exam (75%), which mainly consists of practical exercises and problems, and may include theoretical questions up to 30% of the exam grade. A minimum score of 4.5 out of 10 on the written exam is required to pass the course. Lab practices (20%) require mandatory attendance, submission of exercises, and a minimum score of 3 out of 10 on each lab report; failure to submit reports on time and through PLATEA (not email) will result in not passing. The course is passed or failed in its entirety per call, including theory, problems, and practices. A single evaluation via a 100% weighted exam may be requested only under exceptional circumstances as per Article 13 of the University's Academic Regulations.
